notes: docs/plan/08-rule-catalogue.md is the specification. This file is the single source for the
analyzer's DiagnosticDescriptor, the docs/rules/ page, the `skala explain` text, the SARIF
rules[] block and the ReSharper severity mapping.
ADR-012: an id is allocated once and never re-purposed. RuleCatalogTests.RuleIds_AreAppendOnly
reads Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/allocated-ids.txt and fails the build when an id in it
is absent here or when a shipped id's `concept` changes. Retiring a rule means `retired: true`,
`scope` drives two separate things and they are not the same thing:
- Syntax | Semantic  -> whether the rule may run in --load=loose (docs/plan/07 § loose).
- Compilation        -> excluded from the per-file incremental cache, because its output for
one file depends on files the cache key does not name.
`languageVersion` is a floor and is checked against the compilation's *effective* LangVersion,
never the SDK's. A rule that suggests C# 12 syntax to a project pinned at C# 10 produces

rules.title: The file is not formatted
rules.summary: `skala format` would change this file.
rules.rationale: The formatting half of Skala and the analysis half are one report. A finding that says "this file is not formatted" carries the formatter's own edits as its fix, so a machine reading the SARIF can apply them without a second tool invocation and a human sees formatting and analysis in one list. It is a suggestion rather than a warning because formatting is unconditional and free: the gate that cares is `formatting: clean`, not a severity.

examples.bad: if(x){DoThing();}

rules.falsePositives: None by construction: the finding is produced by running the formatter, so it exists exactly when the formatter has an edit to make. A file that does not parse produces SK9010 instead and is never reported here.
configuration: Every resharper_* formatting key; the finding is whatever the configured formatter does.

rules.title: The line is over the width and nothing in it can break
rules.summary: A line exceeds `max_line_length` and the formatter had no break point to use.
rules.rationale: A 200-character string literal and a deeply-qualified generic type are not the formatter's to shorten: it never breaks a token and never breaks inside a string. Reporting it at hint makes the audit possible without making the ordinary run noisy.

examples.bad: const string Message = "…a literal 200 characters wide…";
examples.good:
const string Message =
    "…the same literal, on a continuation line…";

rules.falsePositives: None. The check is a width measurement of the formatter's own output.

rules.title: The documentation comment is not well-formed XML
rules.summary: A `///` comment does not parse as XML, so it is left exactly as written.
rules.rationale:
Malformed doc comments are common in real code — an unescaped `<`, a `
` borrowed from HTML, a tag someone forgot to close. Skala never repairs them: a formatter that repairs documentation is a formatter that changes what the documentation says. Reporting it is the whole of the response.

examples.bad: /// <summary>Returns x < y.</summary>
examples.good: /// <summary>Returns x < y.</summary>

rules.falsePositives: None known. The check is an XML parse of the comment body.

rules.title: Use a file-scoped namespace
rules.summary: A file with exactly one block-scoped namespace and nothing beside it can use `namespace X;`.
rules.rationale: One level of indentation across every file in the repository, for no expressive gain. The configuration this tool serves already says `csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped`; the rule is what makes that true in code an agent wrote rather than only in code the IDE touched.

examples.good:
namespace Vixen.Core;

public sealed class Archetype;

rules.falsePositives: Only fires when the compilation unit contains exactly one namespace declaration, that namespace is the only member of the unit, it is block-scoped, it contains no nested namespace declaration, and it has no attribute lists or extern aliases after it. A file with two namespaces cannot be converted at all and is not reported; a file whose namespace declaration carries a `#if` inside its braces is skipped, because the conversion moves a brace the disabled branch may own.
rules.resharperNote: ReSharper has no inspection id for this: it drives the conversion from `csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped:suggestion` and reports the result under `resharper_arrange_namespace_body_highlighting = hint`. Two mechanisms, two severities, one concept — so this rule maps to no key at all. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

rules.title: Use `is null` / `is not null` instead of `==` / `!=`
rules.summary: A null comparison written with an operator, on a type that does not define one.
rules.rationale: `x == null` calls whatever `operator ==` the type declares; `x is null` is a pattern and always tests reference (or default) equality. On a type with a user-defined `==` the two are different programs, and on a type without one they are the same program written two ways. Preferring the pattern removes the question. It also survives a later refactor that *adds* an `operator ==`, which is exactly when `== null` silently changes meaning.
rules.falsePositives: The rule is silent unless the semantic model resolves the non-null operand's type and that type declares no `operator ==`/`operator !=`, directly or on any base type. It is silent on unconstrained type parameters (where `== null` has its own lifted meaning), on `dynamic`, on pointer types, on any operand whose type could not be resolved, and inside an expression tree, where the pattern form does not compile.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ A choice, not a derivation. The author's export carries at least six inspections over this ground at four severities: merge_into_pattern (suggestion), arrange_null_checking_pattern (hint), convert_type_check_to_null_check (warning), convert_type_check_pattern_to_null_check (warning), join_null_check_with_usage (suggestion), use_null_propagation (hint). MergeIntoPattern is the closest and the mapping is recorded rather than computed. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

rules.title: Use `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull`
rules.summary: A hand-written null guard that `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` already is.
rules.rationale: The BCL helper is one line instead of three, captures the argument expression itself through `CallerArgumentExpression` so the message cannot drift from the parameter name, and is annotated so the nullable analysis knows the argument is non-null afterwards — which the hand-written form only manages when the `throw` is the whole `if` body.

examples.good: ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source);

rules.falsePositives: Requires `System.ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` to exist in the compilation, so a project on an older target framework is silent rather than offered an uncompilable fix. Only fires when the guard is an `if` whose condition is exactly `x is null` or `x == null` (with the same operator-== check SK1010 makes) and whose body is exactly one `throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(x))` with no message argument and no other statement — a guard that also logs, or that throws a derived exception, or that passes a custom message, is a deliberate choice and is left alone.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_use_throw_if_null_method_highlighting = none`, so reading the key as authoritative would switch this rule off in the repository Skala was built for. That measurement is why --resharper-severities is opt-in. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

rules.title: Use `??=`
rules.rationale: The compound form says the intent once instead of naming the target twice, and it is the form that cannot drift — a rename that misses one of the two occurrences of `x` turns the long form into a silent bug.

examples.bad: _cache = _cache ?? new Dictionary<string, int>();
examples.good: _cache ??= new Dictionary<string, int>();

rules.falsePositives: Only fires when the assignment target and the left operand of the `??` are the *same* expression syntactically, and that expression is a chain of plain identifiers (`x`, `this.x`, `a.b.c`) — never an element access and never anything containing a call, because `a[i] = a[i] ?? b` evaluates the indexer twice and `a[i] ??= b` evaluates it once, which for a side-effecting indexer is a different program.

rules.title: Use the `Count` property, not `Count()` or `Any()`
rules.summary: `list.Count() > 0` and `list.Any()` on something that already has a `Count`.
rules.rationale: `Enumerable.Count()` has a fast path for `ICollection` and `Any()` allocates an enumerator; both are strictly more work than reading the property, and both hide from the reader that the length is already known. The value is legibility more than speed.
rules.falsePositives: Only fires when the invoked method is exactly `System.Linq.Enumerable.Count()` or `Enumerable.Any()` with no argument, the receiver's type has an accessible instance `Count` (or `Length`) property of type `int`, and the receiver expression is a plain identifier or member-access chain with no invocation in it — so `GetItems().Any()` is left alone, because reading `.Count` on it would still call `GetItems()` and the rewrite is only obviously equivalent when the receiver is a variable. Silent on `IQueryable`, where `Any()` is a database round-trip and `Count` is not the same query.
rules.resharperNote: Three inspections cover this ground: use_collection_count_property, replace_with_single_call_to_any and replace_with_single_call_to_count, all `suggestion` in the export. The first is recorded; the mapping is many-to-one from ReSharper's side. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

rules.title: Use `Enum.GetValues<T>()`
rules.summary: `Enum.GetValues(typeof(T))` returns `Array`; the generic overload returns `T[]`.
rules.rationale: The non-generic overload returns `System.Array`, so every caller casts or enumerates as `object` and boxes each member. The generic overload is typed and allocation-free per element, and it is the same call.

examples.bad:
foreach (TokenKind kind in Enum.GetValues(typeof(TokenKind))) {
}
examples.good:
foreach (var kind in Enum.GetValues<TokenKind>()) {
}

rules.falsePositives: Requires the generic `System.Enum.GetValues<T>()` to exist in the compilation, and requires the argument to be a `typeof` naming a type the semantic model resolves to an enum. A `typeof` over a type parameter, over a non-enum, or over anything the model cannot resolve is silent, and so is a call to a user-declared type that happens to be named `Enum`.

rules.title: An exception is constructed and then discarded
rules.summary: `new SomeException(...)` is an expression statement, so the exception is allocated and thrown away.
rules.rationale: Writing `new InvalidOperationException("...");` where `throw new InvalidOperationException("...");` was meant is a guard clause that does nothing. The method continues on the path the author intended to abort, and the failure surfaces later somewhere unrelated. There is no legitimate reason to construct an exception as a standalone statement: an exception object that is neither thrown, returned, assigned nor passed anywhere has no observable effect beyond its own allocation. The fix is the missing keyword.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only on an object-creation expression that *is* the whole of an expression statement, and only when the semantic model resolves the created type and that type derives from `System.Exception`. A constructed exception that is assigned, returned, passed as an argument, added to a collection or used in any other position is not an expression statement and is never seen. Construction whose constructor argument has an intentional side effect is still reported, because the exception is still discarded; that is documented rather than guarded, and no occurrence exists on either reference tree.

rules.title: `throw ex;` resets the stack trace
rules.summary: Re-throwing the caught exception by name restarts its stack trace at the `throw`.
rules.rationale: `throw ex;` inside `catch (Exception ex)` assigns a fresh stack trace to the exception, so every frame between the original throw site and this `catch` is erased. The result is a production log that points at the handler rather than at the fault, which is the one piece of information the log existed to carry. `throw;` re-throws the same exception with its trace intact. The two forms look interchangeable and are not, which is why this is worth a rule rather than a review comment.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only when the thrown expression is a bare identifier whose name is the identifier the *nearest enclosing* catch clause declares, and that name is never assigned anywhere inside the clause. Throwing a different exception, a wrapped exception, an exception belonging to an outer catch clause, a field, a parameter, or a variable the clause reassigned is not this pattern and is not reported. `throw ex;` inside a lambda, a local function or a nested catch clause within the block is excluded, because a bare `throw;` is either illegal or means something else there.

rules.title: `async void` outside an event handler
rules.summary: An `async void` method that nothing subscribes as an event handler.
rules.rationale: An `async void` method cannot be awaited, so its caller cannot know when it finished and cannot observe its exceptions. An exception thrown after the first `await` is raised on whatever synchronization context resumed the method, which in a console or server process means an unhandled exception that terminates it. `async Task` gives the caller both. The one legitimate use is an event handler, whose delegate type returns `void` and whose exceptions the framework expects to handle, so the rule is silent there.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The rule ships disabled — `defaultSeverity: none` — and this is the interesting part of its story rather than a hedge.** It is silent on anything that could be an event handler or is bound to a delegate: an `override`, a `virtual` or `new` method (whose return type binds every override below it), any method implementing an interface member, any method whose name begins `On`, any method with the `(object, EventArgs)` shape, any method carrying an attribute, a partial method, and — the check that costs the most — every method whose name appears anywhere in the compilation in a position other than a direct invocation, which covers `+=` subscription, a method group passed as an argument and a delegate construction. That last check is why the rule is compilation-scoped and can never be served from the per-file incremental cache.

Two measurements decided the default. First, the rule fires **zero** times on both reference trees: Vixen contains no `async void` method at all, and neither does `corpus/real`. Its evidence is therefore three positive and eight negative fixtures and nothing else — a false-positive rate *measured* at zero and *tested* at nothing, which is the distinction docs/plan/16 § R3 is about. Second, enabling it costs every run the warm path of the incremental cache (docs/plan/07 § "The incremental cache"), because a compilation-scoped rule's answer for one file depends on files that file's cache key does not name. Trading the cache for a rule with no measured occurrences is a bad trade to make on someone's behalf, so a repository that has `async void` turns it on deliberately with `dotnet_diagnostic.SK3001.severity = warning` and pays the cost knowing what it bought.
configuration: dotnet_diagnostic.SK3001.severity (`none` by default; set it to `warning` to enable — ⚠ doing so disables the incremental cache's warm path, because the rule is compilation-scoped)
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_async_void_method_highlighting = suggestion` and this rule defaults to `none`. ReSharper's inspection fires on every `async void` including the event handlers, so a low severity is how it stays usable; this rule excludes the event-handler cases by analysis instead, and ships off for the cost reason its `falsePositives` field explains rather than for a noise reason. Reading the ReSharper key — off by default, doc 03 § "Severities" — would turn it on at suggestion.

rules.title: Blocking on an async call
rules.summary: `.Result`, `.Wait()` or `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` on a `Task` or `ValueTask`.
rules.rationale: Blocking a thread on a task is the classic ASP.NET and WPF deadlock: the continuation needs the synchronization context the blocked thread is holding, and neither side moves again. Even where it does not deadlock it consumes a pool thread for the duration, which under load is how a server stops responding to anything at all. It also re-wraps the exception in an `AggregateException`, so the `catch` a reader expects to fire does not. `await` does none of these things.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only when the receiver's type is `System.Threading.Tasks.Task`, `Task<T>`, `ValueTask` or `ValueTask<T>` as resolved by the semantic model — never on a `.Result` property of a user type that happens to be called that, and never when the type did not resolve. It is silent wherever `await` is unavailable or wrong: an entry point, a constructor, a finalizer, an operator, a property or field initializer, a `lock` body, an `unsafe` context, an expression tree, a query clause, and inside a test method, where blocking is deliberate. A fix is offered only where the enclosing method or lambda is *already* `async` and the expression is not inside a `lock`, which is where the rewrite is provably correct; elsewhere the finding is reported with no fix, because making a method `async` changes its signature and therefore its callers, which is not an edit a tool may apply unreviewed.

rules.title: A `Where` the next operator could have taken as its predicate
rules.summary: `xs.Where(p).First()` is `xs.First(p)`: one fewer iterator object and one fewer delegate hop per element.
rules.rationale: `Enumerable.Where` allocates an iterator that the next operator then wraps and drives, so every element crosses two `MoveNext` frames instead of one. `First`, `FirstOrDefault`, `Last`, `LastOrDefault`, `Single`, `SingleOrDefault`, `Any`, `Count` and `LongCount` each have an overload that takes the predicate directly and does the same work in one loop with no intermediate object. LINQ defines the two forms to select the same elements in the same order for the same predicate, so this is a rewrite with no semantic content — which is why it is worth a rule rather than a review comment: the longer form reads no better and costs an indirection per element.

examples.bad:
var first = items.Where(item => item.IsReady).First();
var ready = items.Where(item => item.IsReady).Count();
examples.good:
var first = items.First(item => item.IsReady);
var ready = items.Count(item => item.IsReady);

rules.falsePositives: Both calls must resolve to `System.Linq.Enumerable`. A `Where` or a `First` on `System.Linq.Queryable` is never reported, because a provider is free to translate the one-argument overload and not the predicate one; nor is a user-defined `Where`, a user-defined operator of the same name, or either call when the symbol did not resolve. The `Where` must be the `Func<T, bool>` overload: the indexed `Func<T, int, bool>` form has no counterpart on any of the consuming operators, so it is left alone. The consuming call must pass no arguments of its own and must be one of the nine operators whose predicate overload is defined to iterate identically — `Where(p).All(q)`, `Where(p).Sum(f)` and `Where(p).Select(f)` are different shapes and are not reported. A conditional access (`xs?.Where(p).First()`) is not reported, because the rewrite has to move the member binding rather than replace a name. ⚠ The one observable difference the rewrite does make is the text of the exception on an empty sequence: `Where(p).First()` throws `InvalidOperationException("Sequence contains no elements")` and `First(p)` throws `InvalidOperationException("Sequence contains no matching element")`. The type is the same and the condition is the same; a test asserting on the message string would see the change.

rules.title: Request data is concatenated into SQL
rules.summary: A value that arrived from the request is built into SQL text that a command executes.
rules.rationale: The injected text is not data to the database, it is source code. A single quote in a value ends the literal the query put it in, and everything after it is parsed as more SQL running with the application's own credentials — which is how one search box becomes `DROP TABLE` or a dump of every row the connection can see. The fix is not to escape the quote; escaping is a blocklist and blocklists are wrong at the edges, on every dialect, forever. The fix is to stop concatenating: a parameter is transmitted beside the statement rather than inside it, so the database never parses it as SQL and there is no edge case left to get wrong. Every client has the shape — `command.Parameters.Add`, Dapper's anonymous `param` object, EF Core's `FromSql($"…")` interpolated overload — and all of them are shorter than the concatenation they replace. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic because the edit is not local: introducing a parameter means changing the text, adding a binding, and choosing the parameter's type, which is three decisions rather than a substitution.

examples.bad:
var id = context.Request.Query["id"];
command.CommandText = $"select * from orders where id = {id}";

rules.falsePositives: The rule reports only a flow it can prove inside one method, from a source declared in `taint.json` to a sink declared there, with no sanitizer between them. Everything else is silence, and the exclusions are large on purpose — every one of them is a case where a report would be *wrong*, not merely unwelcome. ⚠ A method parameter is never a source. A parameter's incoming value is whatever the callers pass, which is by definition invisible from inside the method, so treating "unknown" as "suspicious" would assert a vulnerability in code that has none: a private helper ending in `command.CommandText = sql` whose callers all pass a constant with `@name` placeholders and bind properly is completely ordinary, and every report on it would be a false positive. Interpolating a *constant* is not a finding either, so `$"select … from {Schema.VersionTable}"` is silent. ⚠ `Main(string[] args)`, `Console.ReadLine`, `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable` and `File.ReadAllText` are deliberately not sources, because the principal supplying them is the principal the process runs as — there is no boundary being crossed, so there is nothing to inject. Passing a tainted value through `int.Parse` or `Guid.Parse` sanitises it, because the result is not a string. ⚠ Inter-procedural flow is out of scope (docs/plan/08), so a value that reaches the sink through a helper method is a miss rather than a report; so is a sink inside a lambda. Both are the safe direction for a rule that defaults to `error`.

rules.title: Request data reaches a process start
rules.summary: A value that arrived from the request decides which program runs, or what it is told to do.
rules.rationale: `ProcessStartInfo.Arguments` is a single string that the child process re-splits on its own rules, so a quote or an ampersand in the value is not data — it is punctuation in somebody else's grammar, and the result is a second command running as this process's user. `FileName` is worse: it chooses the program. The replacement for `Arguments` is `ArgumentList`, which passes each element to the child verbatim — exec takes an array on Unix, and on Windows .NET does the quoting itself — so there is no syntax left to escape and no shell involved. The replacement for a tainted `FileName` is a `switch` over the programs this code is allowed to run, returning the constant path for each; an allow-list is the only thing that works, because deciding whether an arbitrary path is safe to execute is not a question with an answer. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic: moving one `Arguments` string into `ArgumentList` means splitting a command line, which is exactly the parsing this rule exists to avoid guessing at.

examples.bad:
var file = context.Request.Query["file"];
Process.Start("convert", "-resize 100x100 " + file);

rules.falsePositives: The rule shares its engine and therefore its whole exclusion story with `SK5001`: a proven intra-procedural flow from a declared source only, a parameter is never a source, and unknown is never a guess. ⚠ The exclusion that matters most here is that argv is not a source, and it is a statement about where the trust boundary is rather than about finding counts. A tool that starts a program at the path its user typed is doing its job; the party supplying argv is the party the process runs as, so there is no boundary to cross and a report would be asserting a vulnerability that does not exist. ⚠ `ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList` is deliberately not a sink even when what is added to it is tainted: it is the fix this rule recommends, and reporting it would mean telling a reader that the remedy is also the disease. Argument content that the *child program* interprets — a leading `@` or `-` that some tools read as a file reference — is outside the rule, because it depends on a program Skala cannot see.

rules.title: A broken cipher, or a mode that leaks structure
rules.summary: `DES`, `TripleDES`, `RC2` or ECB mode — none of them hides a plaintext any more.
rules.rationale: `DES` has a 56-bit key, which was already marginal when it was standardised and is exhaustively searched in hours on hardware anyone can rent. `TripleDES` fixed the key length and not the 64-bit block, so a collision becomes likely after about 32 GB under one key and the plaintext starts coming back out — that is CVE-2016-2183, "Sweet32", and it is a practical attack on a long TLS connection rather than a theoretical one. `RC2` has practical key-recovery attacks. ECB is a different failure and a more visible one: it encrypts equal blocks to equal ciphertext, so the shape of the input survives encryption — the standard demonstration is a bitmap of a penguin that is still obviously a penguin afterwards. Use `Aes`, and prefer `AesGcm`, which authenticates the ciphertext as well as hiding it, so an attacker cannot flip bits in a message you will decrypt and act on. ⚠ There is no fix, and that is deliberate: swapping the algorithm compiles and changes the key length, the block size and the ciphertext format, so everything already encrypted becomes unreadable. That is a data migration, not an edit.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ The id was allocated narrower than docs/plan/08's sentence for it, and the reason is that the other half cannot be decided correctly. The catalogue wrote "weak hash/cipher (`MD5`, `SHA1`, `DES`, ECB)" and the hash half was cut — not for firing too often, which would be work for the repository rather than a defect in the rule, but because the finding would frequently be *wrong*. `MD5` and `SHA-1` have a large legitimate population in which they are not security controls at all: cache keys, ETags, content addressing, bucket selection, and every wire protocol that froze its digest choice a decade ago and specifies it normatively — an RFC 6455 WebSocket handshake is *defined* as a SHA-1 of the client key and a fixed GUID, and reporting it would assert a vulnerability in code that cannot have one. Separating that population from a password digest needs to know what the hash is compared against and what happens when it matches, which is a question about the value's use that this rule does not ask and that an intra-procedural engine could not answer if it did. ADR-012 forbids widening an id later, so the hash half needs its own number — and an argument about how it will decide the question — before it is built. What ships fires only on a type deriving from `DES`, `TripleDES` or `RC2`, and on `CipherMode.ECB` as the value assigned to a cipher's `Mode`, so `if (algorithm.Mode == CipherMode.ECB) throw` is silent: that is the guard, not the bug. A `DES` implementation kept only to decrypt an old archive is a true finding and an unwelcome one; that is what a baseline entry is for, and it is not a reason to soften the rule.

rules.title: A certificate callback that accepts everything
rules.summary: A TLS validation callback that returns `true` without looking makes the connection encrypted but unauthenticated.
rules.rationale: TLS gives you two things and they are separable: the traffic is encrypted, and the party at the other end is who the certificate says. A callback that returns `true` for every input keeps the first and throws away the second — so the connection is perfectly encrypted, to whoever answered. That is the whole content of a man-in-the-middle attack: an attacker on the path presents any certificate at all, this code accepts it, and reads and rewrites everything in both directions while both ends see a padlock. Deleting the callback restores the platform's validation, which is chain building, revocation, hostname matching and the trust store, and is years of work nobody should reimplement. If one specific self-signed certificate genuinely has to be trusted — a device on a factory network, a local development server — then pin it: compare `certificate.GetCertHashString()` against the one thumbprint you mean and return `false` for every other input. That is four lines, it is auditable, and it fails closed when the wrong certificate shows up.

examples.bad: handler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback = (_, _, _, _) => true;

rules.falsePositives: Two conditions must both hold, and both are decided without following anything. The target has to be a delegate that returns `bool` and takes a `System.Net.Security.SslPolicyErrors` — which is how the rule covers `ServicePointManager.ServerCertificateValidationCallback`, `HttpClientHandler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback`, `SslClientAuthenticationOptions.RemoteCertificateValidationCallback` and the `SslStream` constructor argument without naming any of them, and how a fifth spelling arrives covered. And the value has to be provably constant-`true`: an expression body that is the literal `true`, a block whose one statement is `return true;`, or `HttpClientHandler.DangerousAcceptAnyServerCertificateValidator`. ⚠ A callback with any condition in it is silence — a thumbprint comparison, an `errors == SslPolicyErrors.None` test, a method group, a field holding a delegate. Following those is the inter-procedural analysis docs/plan/08 puts out of scope, and a wrong `error` here would fail a build over a pinning implementation. ⚠ The most common true finding is a test or a local development environment talking to a self-signed certificate, and the rule ships at `error` anyway. That is not the same situation as `SK8005`'s polling `Thread.Sleep`, which is correct code the rule cannot recognise; this is never correct code, it is an accepted risk — and an accepted risk has a way of reaching production inside a `#if` that stopped being conditional. Accept it deliberately and visibly: a baseline entry, or a `#pragma` with a justification comment. ⚠ Nothing enforces that comment today — `SK7050` is allocated in docs/plan/08 and unbuilt — so the baseline, whose diff somebody reads, is the disposal with a mechanism behind it. Not a lower severity.

rules.title: An XML reader that parses a DTD and fetches what it names
rules.summary: DTD processing plus a resolver that goes to the network or the disk is XXE.
rules.rationale: A DTD can declare an entity whose value is a URI, and a reader with a resolver will go and get it — so a document the process was merely asked to parse can read any file that process can read and reach any host it can reach, and hand the contents back inside the parsed result or out through an error message. That is XXE, and it turns an XML endpoint into a file-read and a request-forgery primitive at once. Two settings control it and either one closes the hole: `XmlResolver = null` keeps DTD parsing working for internal entities while resolving nothing external, and `DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit` refuses the DTD outright, which is right when the documents are not supposed to have one. ⚠ There is no fix, because which of those two is correct depends on whether the documents legitimately carry a DTD — a question about the data, not about the code.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ The rule needs two facts where docs/plan/08's sentence named one, and the platform is why. On .NET Framework `DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Parse` was enough, because the default `XmlResolver` was an `XmlUrlResolver`. On .NET Core and later the default resolver is `null`, so parsing a DTD resolves nothing external and is not XXE — a rule that fired on `DtdProcessing.Parse` alone would report, at `error` severity, every program that legitimately parses a document with entity declarations, on a platform where that is not a vulnerability. So the rule fires only where the resolver is put back *and* the DTD is parsed. Both assignments must be explicit, both must be about the same object, and both must be in the same method: a resolver assigned from a variable is silence, because whether that variable is null is a question about another method, and `XmlSecureResolver` is excluded by name because it is the mitigation. The cost of the strictness is coverage — the shape occurs zero times in either reference tree. ⚠ Known gap, stated rather than hidden: `XmlDocument` and `XmlDataDocument` have an `XmlResolver` and no `DtdProcessing`, so the two-fact rule cannot see them and they are outside it; closing that needs its own id rather than a widening of this one.

rules.title: An abstract type has a public constructor
rules.summary: Nothing outside the type hierarchy can call it, so `public` on it states something that is not true.
rules.rationale: An abstract class cannot be instantiated, so its constructor is reachable only from a derived constructor's initializer — which is exactly what `protected` allows. Written `public`, the modifier claims a caller that cannot exist, and a reader scanning the type for its public surface has to work out that this member is not part of it. `protected` says what the constructor is for. The edit is one keyword, it removes nothing any caller could have been using, and it is verified by the compiler.
rules.falsePositives: The rule is purely syntactic and fires only on a constructor declared exactly `public` inside a `class` declaration that carries the `abstract` modifier in the same file. A `protected internal`, `internal` or `private protected` constructor is left alone, because each of those is a deliberate statement about a different audience. A static constructor has no accessibility to change. Records are not reported at all: a positional record's primary constructor is a parameter list with no `ConstructorDeclarationSyntax` to edit, and a record's copy constructor has accessibility rules of its own that the compiler enforces (CS8878), so the one-keyword edit is not obviously legal there. A partial class whose `abstract` modifier sits on a different part is a miss rather than a wrong answer — the rule needs to see the modifier beside the constructor. A constructor whose `public` token carries a preprocessor directive in its trivia is skipped, because the token the fix replaces may not exist in every branch.

rules.title: Cyclomatic complexity is over the threshold
rules.summary: The number of linearly independent paths through a member, from its control-flow graph.
rules.rationale: Cyclomatic complexity counts the decision points in a body, and it is the number that predicts how many test cases the body needs to cover. It is computed from Roslyn's `ControlFlowGraph` rather than by counting keywords, so a `switch` expression, a pattern with a `when` clause, a conditional access chain and a `&&` short-circuit are each counted the way the compiler sees them rather than the way a regular expression would. It is the least interesting of the metrics on its own — a long flat `switch` scores high and reads fine — which is why it defaults to `hint` and why cognitive complexity is the one the gate reads.

examples.bad: // a member whose control-flow graph has 40 conditional edges
examples.good: // the same logic split across members, or expressed as a table

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface.

rules.title: Cognitive complexity is over the threshold
rules.summary: How hard a member is to read, by Sonar's published definition: nesting-weighted, with no penalty for a `switch`.
rules.rationale: Cognitive complexity is the metric worth gating on, and it is the one SonarQube users actually miss. It differs from cyclomatic complexity in the two ways that matter: a `switch` over twenty cases costs one, because a reader takes it in at a glance, and a condition nested three deep costs four rather than one, because a reader has to hold three contexts to understand it. That makes it track the thing people mean by "this method is hard" rather than the thing that is easy to count. The implementation follows Sonar's specification — increments for each control-flow break, a nesting increment for each structure nested inside another, one increment per sequence of like binary operators, and increments for `goto`, recursion and each `catch` — so a number here is comparable to a number from SonarQube on the same code.
rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface. The default threshold is 15, which is Sonar's own and the number doc 09's `ci` gate names.

rules.title: The member is over the statement-count threshold
rules.summary: Method length counted in statements, not in lines.
rules.rationale: Counting lines makes the metric a function of the formatter: the same body scores differently at a 100-column width and at a 160-column one, and wrapping a long argument list makes a method "longer" without changing anything a reader has to understand. Counting statements is invariant under formatting, which is the property that makes the number worth putting in a gate at all. Declarations, expression statements, and each statement nested inside a block are counted once each; a `for` header is one statement, not three.

examples.bad: // a 300-statement method
examples.good: // the same work as several members with names

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface.

rules.title: The type is over the member-count threshold
rules.summary: Members declared on a type, with fields counted separately.
rules.rationale: A type's member count is the crudest of the metrics and still the one that finds god objects. Fields are counted separately from methods because the two mean different things: forty fields is a data carrier, which may be exactly right, while forty methods is a type doing forty jobs. The report carries both numbers and the rule fires on the member count. A partial type is measured per declaration rather than per symbol, because that is the file a person opens.

examples.bad: // a type with 200 methods
examples.good: // the same surface split along the seams the names already suggest

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface. Enum members are not counted: a 300-member enum is a table, not a god object.

rules.title: The member takes more parameters than the threshold
rules.summary: Parameter count, including a primary constructor's parameters.
rules.rationale: A long parameter list is the one design smell that is unambiguous from the outside: past about seven the call sites stop being readable and start being positional puzzles, and every one of them has to change when the list does. Primary-constructor parameters count, because they are the type's constructor whatever the syntax; doc 07 § Metrics says so explicitly.

examples.bad: void Configure(int a, int b, int c, int d, int e, int f, int g, int h) { }
examples.good: void Configure(in ConfigureOptions options) { }

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface. A `this` parameter on an extension method is counted, because a caller supplies it. Generated code is excluded, which matters here: a generated `record`'s positional constructor and a DI factory's constructor are both routinely wide and neither is a design decision anybody made.

rules.title: The member nests deeper than the threshold
rules.summary: The deepest block nesting inside a member body.
rules.rationale: Nesting depth is what cognitive complexity's nesting weight is built on, reported on its own because it is the actionable half: a body six levels deep almost always has an early return or a `continue` that flattens it, and a reader can see that from the number without reading the body. A lambda body restarts the count, because a lambda is a separate reading context.
rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface.

rules.title: Public API without a documentation comment
rules.summary: Doc-comment coverage of the publicly visible surface, reported as a metric and — opt-in — as a finding.
rules.rationale: Comment density is the metric most likely to be gamed and the one most worth having as a *number* rather than as a finding. As an aggregate it says whether a library's public surface is documented; as a per-member warning on a repository that has never documented anything it produces thousands of findings on day one and gets switched off by lunchtime. So it ships disabled — `defaultSeverity: none` — and a repository that wants it turns it on for the paths where it means something, exactly the way doc 08 § SK1000 describes for the hot-path rules. The aggregate is computed either way and appears in the report and in `skala trend`.
rules.falsePositives: Disabled by default, so it produces nothing until a repository asks for it. When enabled it counts only members that are publicly visible through their whole containing chain, ignores accessors, explicit interface implementations, operators, finalizers, compiler-generated members, `record` positional members and anything in generated code, and treats an `<inheritdoc/>` as documentation.
configuration: dotnet_diagnostic.SK7010.severity (`none` by default; set it per path to enable)

rules.title: Duplicated block
rules.summary: A run of at least `minTokens` tokens that occurs identically, up to identifier and literal names, somewhere else in the repository.
rules.rationale: Duplication is the one SonarQube feature with no Roslyn equivalent, and the AI workflow needs it more than most: agents copy-paste by nature, and a block pasted four times is four places a fix has to land. Detection is token-level type-2 clone detection — identifiers and literals normalised to a class, keywords and punctuation kept exact — so a block copied and renamed is still found, which is the copy people actually make. A clone group is reported once, at its first occurrence, with the rest as related locations; reporting it at every occurrence would turn one problem into n findings and make the count meaningless.

examples.bad: // the same 100-token block, pasted into four files with the variables renamed
examples.good: // one method, called four times

rules.falsePositives: Not a false-positive-prone rule in the usual sense — a reported group either is or is not a token-for-token match, and the match is verified exactly rather than trusted from the rolling hash, so a hash collision cannot produce a finding. What it can do is report duplication that is deliberate. Three exclusions handle the cases that matter and are the whole of the rule's tuning: generated files are excluded from the findings and from both halves of the percentage; test files are measured but counted and reported separately, because duplication in tests is often the readable choice and gating it drives people to write worse tests; and the 100-token default is Sonar's own for C#, which is roughly 25 lines and well above the length of any idiomatic boilerplate.

rules.title: `Thread.Sleep` in a test
rules.summary: A test that waits for a duration passes or fails on how loaded the machine is.
rules.rationale: A sleep encodes a guess about how long the thing under test takes. On a developer's idle laptop the guess holds; on a CI agent running sixteen jobs it does not, and the test fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the code. The failure is intermittent, so it is triaged as flakiness rather than as a defect, and a suite with a few of these stops being read at all. It also costs the sleep on every run, forever, including all the runs where the wait was not needed. What the test wants is a signal — a handle, a task, a callback, a polled predicate with a generous timeout — and every one of those is both faster and deterministic. ⚠ There is no fix: the replacement is a change to what the test synchronises on, which is a design decision and not an edit.
rules.falsePositives: The rule fires only where the semantic model resolves the call to `System.Threading.Thread.Sleep`, so a `Sleep` method on a user type of that name is never reported, and neither is anything at all when the symbol did not resolve. It is scoped by attribute rather than by path: the call must sit lexically inside a method carrying a recognised test attribute (`Fact`, `Theory`, `Test`, `TestCase`, `TestMethod`, `Benchmark`), which is the same set `SK3002` uses, so a sleep in a helper method a test calls, in a fixture's constructor, or anywhere in production code is outside the rule. ⚠ A `[Benchmark]` method counts as a test method for this rule because the shared helper says so; a deliberate sleep in a benchmark is the shape most likely to be reported and not wanted. The rule cannot tell a sleep that is a guess from a sleep that is the point of the test — a test of a frame limiter, a debounce, or a file watcher's coalescing window has to advance a real clock, and reports there are true and unwanted. That is what the default severity of `suggestion` and a baseline are for; a repository that wants the rule to bite promotes it in the `[**/*.Tests/**/*.cs]` section its `.editorconfig` already has.

rules.title: Unknown configuration key
rules.summary: A key in the `.editorconfig` chain is not in the option registry.
rules.rationale: The Rider export carries roughly two thousand keys Skala will never implement. Reporting them at suggestion rather than warning is the difference between an audit and an uninstall.

examples.bad: resharper_cpp_indent_size = 2

rules.falsePositives: Any key outside the registry, which includes every C++, VB and XAML key in the export. That is why it is not a warning.

rules.title: The file does not parse
rules.summary: The file has parse errors, so it is reported and left byte-identical.
rules.rationale: ADR-003, and the single most important safety property in the tool: a file Skala cannot parse is a file Skala does not touch.

examples.bad: class C { void M( }
examples.good: class C { void M() { } }

rules.falsePositives: None. The check is Roslyn's own error diagnostics.

rules.title: A member's braces are split across a preprocessor branch
rules.summary: The member is emitted verbatim, because its brace structure depends on which branch is active.
rules.rationale: Roslyn parses one branch and hands back a tree describing only that one. Reindenting from it moves braces the other branch owns.
rules.falsePositives: None known; the check counts braces per branch and only fires when the branches disagree.

rules.title: The binlog is stale for this file
rules.summary: The file on disk differs from what the recorded build compiled; the current text was substituted.
rules.rationale: Analysing what the build saw rather than what is on disk would report findings against code nobody has. Substituting the current text keeps the report about the working tree and says so.
rules.falsePositives: None; it is a comparison of file content against the compilation's recorded source list.

rules.title: The binlog does not name a file that exists
rules.summary: A `.cs` file under the repository is in no recorded compilation. Rebuild.
rules.rationale: A new file that the binlog does not name is invisible to every compilation and is therefore silently unanalysed, which is the worst failure this tool can have. It is a warning and not an info for exactly that reason.
rules.falsePositives: A file genuinely excluded from compilation — a scratch file, a `.cs` under a directory with `EnableDefaultCompileItems=false` — is reported too. `skala.jsonc`'s `exclude` is the answer, and the message names the file.

rules.title: An analyzer threw
rules.summary: An analyzer raised an exception; it is disabled for the rest of the run and everything else continues.
rules.rationale: A third-party analyzer that throws on one syntax shape must not be able to turn a CI gate red for unrelated reasons — or, worse, green by aborting the run early.
rules.falsePositives: None; it reports an exception that happened.

rules.title: An analyzer package failed to load
rules.summary: A hosted analyzer package named in `skala.jsonc` could not be loaded. Never fatal.
rules.rationale: ADR-008: third-party rules are hosted, never bundled. A package that is missing, is for another framework, or drags a conflicting dependency is a configuration problem to report, not a reason to produce no report at all.
rules.falsePositives: None; it reports a load that failed.

rules.title: The formatter's output was not token-equivalent
rules.summary: A Skala bug by definition. Nothing was written and a reproduction was dropped under `.skala/crash/`.
rules.rationale: ADR-005. The check is one extra parse per file, it costs about 15 % of formatting time, and there is no flag that turns it off.
rules.falsePositives: None. A finding here is a bug in Skala.
